name: Iceve-Maci
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Cox, Bruce. 2013. A Phonological Overview of Iceve-Maci. Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon (Ministry of Scientific Research and Innovation). 75 pp. (77 pp.). SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 53984.
catalog_locator: §9 'Stress', p. 49; fn. 69 in §7.2 'Final vowel deletion', p. 38; §8 'Tone', p. 41; see also §4 'Syllable Structure', p. 19 ('these are prominent, "stressed"') and §3.5 'Distribution', p. 16 ('the more prominent V1 root-positions').
catalog_quote: Stress in Iceve-Maci generally falls on the first stem syllable, but does not have a very prominent realisation. Stress does not play a highly significant role in the phonology. There are nevertheless a few observations that may be related to stress. • Final Vowel Deletion does not apply to the “stressed” syllable (see §7.2, in particular footnote 69). • CGV syllables were posited in §4 to account for palatalised and labialised phones in some stem-initial surface structures. This additional contrast is consistent with this being the stressed or prominent position in the word. • The realisation of the suffixes of noun classes 7, 8, 12 and 15 are realised more distinctively when affixed to a CV root than to the less prominent second syllable of a CVCV root, as described in §6.1. • Similarly, velar plosives K in the sequence /Ke/ tend to be realised with palatalised phones monosyllabic (and therefore generally stem-initial) roots (e.g., /ⁿɡe/ [ŋɡje] carry), as described in §2.2. [§9, p. 49] ... Stress falls on the stem-initial syllable; Final Vowel Deletion is perhaps limited to unstressed vowels. [fn. 69, p. 38] ... Iceve-Maci is a tonal language. It has two contrastive tone levels, High and Low. [§8, p. 41]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Iceve-Maci is a two-level (H/L) tone language. Stress, weakly realised and phonologically marginal, falls on the first syllable of the stem (root), i.e. the syllable after any noun-class prefix — a morphologically anchored stem-initial position rather than word-initial. Evidence offered is indirect: final-vowel deletion spares the stem-initial syllable; the extra CGV contrast and palatalised velars are confined to stem-initial syllables; noun-class suffixes are realised more distinctly after CV than after CVCV roots. If a positional code is wanted the closest is morphologically determined (stem-initial).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author hedges ('generally', 'not a very prominent realisation', 'does not play a highly significant role', observations that 'may be related to stress').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word; stems with class prefixes/suffixes), based on elicited data from the Oliti dialect collected 2008-2013 in Enjawbaw village, Cameroon; Becheve dialect only touched on segmentally. No instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: Cox 2013 describes the Oliti dialect of Iceve-Maci (spoken mainly in Cameroon; data from Ogalawen quarter, Enjawbaw village, Manyu Division), with only segmental notes on the Becheve dialect (Nigeria and three villages near Akwaya). Glottolog 5.3 treats Iceve-Maci [icev1238] as a single language; I did not verify whether it assigns dialect-level glottocodes to Oliti or Becheve.

tone_statements.citation: Cox, Bruce. 2014. Tone in the Iceve Verb. Yaoundé: SIL. 64 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Iceve verb roots exhibit a two-way lexical tone contrast between High-tone roots and toneless roots … As will be seen, High-tone roots are always realised with a High tone on the root. Toneless roots are usually realised with a Low tone on the root, but CV roots in some forms emerge with a High tone. … Iceve appears to be a “movable” tone language. It has just two contrastive tone levels. Its words, while not long, are certainly not the monosyllables typical of “stable” tone languages, and the lexical functional load is arguably relatively light.
tone_statements.locator: p. 14, §4.1 'Lexical tone contrast' with fn. 22, and p. 28, §5 'Towards an orthography of tone in verbs'
tone_statements.summary: Two contrastive tone levels, High and Low; verb roots contrast High vs toneless (surface Low); falling contours derived; downstepped High and floating tones in verb morphology; nothing on word stress.
